title: The repeat rejection reasons could be caught before verification

children.text: KYB approval was falling while submission volume was also weakening. I did not want to improve approval by adding another mandatory step that made the flow harder to finish.

I started with rejection data and quick interviews with several merchants who had been rejected. The three most common problems were mismatches between business information and the storefront photo, product photo, or business name.
Some cases came from guidance that was missed or misunderstood. Others genuinely needed checking because the uploaded image or business name did not clearly represent the business being registered.

callout: The goal was to catch likely mismatches earlier without letting AI decide whether a merchant should be approved or rejected.

description: These numbers come from the period after launch and are treated as production evidence rather than a controlled experiment.

title: The early evidence pointed to a specific class of problems
description: I used these three views to decide what should be checked, where the check belonged in the flow, and how model findings should become product logic.

tabs.label: Approval trend
tabs.title: Approval was already moving in the wrong direction

tabs.caption: Baseline context before the pre-check was introduced.

tabs.label: Rejection reasons
tabs.title: Three mismatch reasons kept recurring
tabs.description: The recurring problems involved business information, storefront photos, product photos, and business names.

tabs.caption: These mismatches became the first target for the pre-check.

tabs.title: A model finding was not yet a merchant message

title: Better guidance helped, but it still could not inspect a submission
description: The interviews showed that guidance needed work. The rejection data also showed cases where the actual submission needed to be checked before it was sent.

left.label: Guidance improvement
left.title: Make the existing guide easier to find
left.description: Useful when a merchant does not know what a valid photo should look like. The guide still cannot tell whether the uploaded image matches the business being registered.

right.label: AI-assisted pre-check
right.title: Check likely mismatches while the merchant can still fix them
right.description: Use the business information and photos already available in Step 1 to show a warning before the application reaches verification.
right.note: AstraPay already had Llama available through Vertex AI, which made this a more practical option to ship quickly.

title: AI sits before submission, not at the final decision
description: This flow separates the responsibilities of the merchant, product layer, Vertex AI, and verification.

lanes.label: Merchant
lanes.description: Provides the input and decides whether a finding needs correction.

lanes.label: KYB product
lanes.description: Controls when the pre-check runs and how findings are presented.

lanes.label: Vertex AI
lanes.description: Checks the mismatch conditions defined for the pre-check.

lanes.label: Verification
lanes.description: Keeps ownership of the final KYB decision.

nodes.label: Enter business information and upload photos
nodes.description: Business name, category, storefront photo, and product photo already exist in the KYB flow.

nodes.label: Run the pre-check
nodes.description: The product layer sends the relevant inputs before the merchant submits.

nodes.label: Check targeted mismatches
nodes.description: The model looks for likely inconsistencies across the business information and photos.

nodes.label: Map findings to product rules
nodes.description: Technical output becomes stable conditions and merchant-facing feedback.

nodes.label: Is there a finding that needs review?
nodes.description: A warning only appears when a defined condition needs the merchant's attention.

nodes.label: Fix the input or continue
nodes.description: The merchant can correct the flagged input or continue when they believe the submission is already right.

nodes.label: Submit KYB
nodes.description: The application enters the normal verification process.

nodes.description: The AI pre-check does not replace verification.

note: AI only provides a finding before submission. Verification still decides whether the merchant is approved or rejected.

title: The model can stay specific while the merchant message stays simple
description: The same photo problem can be described in several ways by the model. The product needs one stable instruction that a merchant can act on.

left.label: Model finding
left.title: Keep the detail for product logic
left.description: The model might describe a dark image, an interior-only photo, an unclear storefront, or a storefront that is not visible.
left.note: This detail is useful for mapping, evaluation, and debugging.

right.label: Merchant message
right.title: Show one clear correction
right.description: Those findings can map to one instruction asking the merchant to adjust the storefront photo according to the guide.
right.note: The merchant only needs to know what to fix.

title: Try the AI-assisted pre-check
description: The warning is assistive. A merchant can fix the flagged input or continue when they believe the submission is already correct.

title: AI was deliberately kept as an assistive layer
description: The first release kept the decision boundary clear while the quality of the findings still needed monitoring.

title: Prompt design became a contract between the model and the product

children.text: I worked with the developer on the prompt, condition definitions, and output structure. The response needed to be predictable enough for the product layer to map it to the right message and next action.
Prompt detail only helped when it improved a decision the product could use. Output that was too open-ended made the mapping harder to maintain and made incorrect findings harder to evaluate.

callout: The model produces a finding. The product still decides how that finding changes the merchant experience.

title: The strongest evidence sits in the rejection reasons the pre-check directly targeted

children.text: After launch, the three targeted mismatch remarks fell by 22–90%. Approval also improved by around 7%, while submission volume remained relatively stable.

The movement in targeted remarks is closest to the mechanism of the pre-check because those are the conditions it directly inspects. I treat the approval improvement as directional post-launch evidence rather than causal proof from a controlled experiment.

callout: The strongest link is with the targeted rejection reasons, not a claim that the entire approval improvement came from the AI pre-check.

title: I would expand the model's role only after measuring its errors more closely

children.text: The next step is a stronger evaluation set that makes false positives and false negatives visible for each condition. That gives the team a better basis for comparing models and deciding which warnings are reliable enough to become firmer.
For more specialized visual checks, I would also compare the LLM with computer vision or a hybrid approach. Not every image problem needs to be handled by one model.
